description: Hi! I’m Md. Ahsan Munna, a CSE undergrad interested in backend, ML and DL. I know C, C++, Python, Java and ML. First time at Space Apps, I want to learn and build something great. We’ll build a web app to browse NASA’s CLPS lunar missions. I’ll handle backend and data. Looking for a frontend developer (HTML/CSS/JS/React), a UI/UX designer, and anyone into data visualization or presentations. Beginners welcome!
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a browser tool for comparing Moon south pole landing sites and dates, built for mission planners, educators and the public. For 6,313 grid sites inside NASA's nine Artemis III candidate regions, it uses NASA LOLA topography to trace each site's terrain horizon and NAIF SPICE ephemerides to place the Sun and Earth as discs against it, for any window in 2027–2029. It reports illumination availability, longest darkness and geometric Earth visibility, and compares configurations side by side with no single "best" score, because power, communications and terrain safety trade off. A Python engine precomputes a 12 MB data pack, so the app runs entirely in the browser with no server. This matters because near the pole the Sun and Earth stay close to the horizon, so nearby terrain decides whether a site is lit and in contact.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
The app lets a user choose one of NASA's nine Artemis III candidate landing regions on the Moon's south pole, a site on a 1 km grid inside it (6,313 sites in total), an observer height (1 m or 5 m) and a date window from 7 to 365 days between 2027 and 2029. It then shows the terrain horizon seen from that site, with the Sun and Earth drawn as discs at true angular size so that a half-hidden Sun looks half hidden. A time slider moves both discs across the terrain. For the chosen window it reports illumination availability, Sun visible (any part), longest continuous darkness, geometric Earth visibility (any part of the disc, and more than half of it) and the longest Earth-visibility blackout. The site map can be coloured by Sun illumination or Earth visibility, two buttons jump to the highest-value site in a region, and up to three configurations can be compared side by side. There is deliberately no overall score.

HOW IT WORKS
1. NASA LOLA 20 m south polar topography gives ground height and slope. For each site and height we trace terrain rays in 360 directions (20 m resolution near the site, 160 m farther out, with lunar curvature) to build a horizon profile.
2. NAIF SPICE (DE440 ephemeris, lunar orientation, MOON_ME frame) gives Moon-centred Sun and Earth positions every 15 minutes for 2027–2029.
3. A Python engine precomputes a 12 MB data pack. The browser then turns each position into azimuth, elevation and angular size for the selected site and computes the visible fraction of each disc against the horizon, entirely client-side (vanilla JavaScript, Canvas 2D, no third-party scripts).

BENEFITS
It turns specialist astrodynamics and terrain analysis into something a planner, student or teacher can explore in minutes, and it makes the trade-offs between power and communication visible instead of hiding them behind a score.

HOW WE CHECKED IT
The SPICE geometry reproduces the sub-solar and sub-Earth points of a NASA LRO reference at one epoch; a deep crater site comes out fully dark; the browser engine matches the Python engine on 12 reference cases (illumination within 0.005, angles within 0.01 degrees); and a 56-test suite covers geometry, SPICE and data-pack integrity. We ignore light-time and aberration, which we measured with SPICE at 0.006 degrees for the Sun and 0.0002 degrees for Earth, far below the 0.53 degree solar disc.


LIMITS (stated in the app)
Earth visibility is geometric line of sight, not a radio link budget. Region centres are approximate (placed from an annotated screenshot of NASA's map). The 20 m DEM cannot resolve rocks or small craters, and sites on steep rims are sensitive to terrain within about 100 m. We have not yet compared results with NASA's published illumination maps.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE
A transparent, open tool for early site comparison, and a base to extend: benchmarking against NASA PGDA illumination and Earth-visibility products, official region boundaries, custom locations, slope and roughness layers, and a link-budget model.

TOOLS
Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, SpiceyPy, Matplotlib, pytest), JavaScript (ES modules, Canvas 2D), Node.js (tests), Git and GitHub, GitHub Pages, VS Code, Google Antigravity and Claude (see the SI section).

LINKS
Live app: https://ahsanmunna.me/lunar-landing-site-navigator/web/index.html
Source code (Apache-2.0), tests, documentation and AI log: https://github.com/ahsanmunna/lunar-landing-site-navigator
dataRefs: NASA LOLA LDEM_80S_20MPP_ADJ south polar DEM (PGDA, Barker et al. 2023)
NAIF SPICE de440.bsp planetary and lunar ephemeris
NAIF SPICE moon_de440_220930.tf MOON_ME frame kernel
